title: IP Ratings Explained: What IP67, IP68, IP54 and IPX8 Mean
description: How to read the two digits, what the laboratory tests do and do not cover, why foldables carry different ratings, and how water resistance degrades over time.
content:
An IP rating looks like a promise and functions like a footnote. The two digits after "IP" describe exactly what was tested, in a laboratory, under conditions that rarely match the way phones are actually dropped. Knowing how to read them - and what they leave out - is the difference between buying water resistance and buying peace of mind.

## Reading the two digits

The format is IP followed by two digits: the first covers solids (dust and objects), the second covers liquids.

**First digit (dust and objects):**

- 4 - protected against objects larger than 1 mm, such as wire. Not dust-tight.
- 5 - dust ingress limited; some dust can enter but not enough to interfere with operation.
- 6 - dust-tight. No ingress of dust under test conditions.
- X - no dust test performed at all. The X is not a zero; it means the claim was never made.

**Second digit (liquids):**

- 4 - protected against splashing water from any direction.
- 5 - protected against water jets from a nozzle.
- 6 - protected against powerful water jets.
- 7 - immersion in fresh water up to 1 metre for up to 30 minutes.
- 8 - immersion beyond 1 metre, for a duration and depth the manufacturer specifies. This is the important nuance: IPx8 is manufacturer-defined, so the depth is not standardized between brands.
- 9 - high-pressure, high-temperature jets. Rare on phones; you will see it as IP69 or IP69K.

An IPX8 phone therefore has a meaningful water rating and no dust rating at all - a common combination where a mechanism (a hinge, a port cover) prevents a dust-tight claim.

## What the tests actually are

All of these tests are laboratory procedures: clean fresh water, specified temperature, specified pressure or depth, specified duration, on an undamaged unit. They are not a simulation of a swimming pool, a shower, the sea or a pocket full of sand.

Two consequences follow. Salt water, chlorine, soap, shampoo and heat all attack seals differently from the fresh water used in testing. And a phone that has been dropped - even one that still looks fine - may no longer meet the rating it shipped with, because a slightly deformed frame compresses a gasket unevenly. Manufacturers commonly exclude liquid damage from warranties regardless of the rating printed on the box.

## What our database shows

The 47 phones we track carry a spread of ratings that illustrates why one number never tells the whole story:

- **IP68** on 23 phones - the flagship standard: dust-tight plus immersion beyond 1 metre as specified by the maker.
- **IP67** on 4 phones - dust-tight plus immersion to 1 metre for 30 minutes. Still submersion-rated.
- **IPX8** on 4 phones - immersion rated, no dust test claimed.
- **IP48** on 4 phones - objects over 1 mm plus immersion. This is the foldable combination.
- **IP54, IP52 and IPX4** on budget and splash-focused models - splash or jet protection, with no immersion claim (and, for the X rating, no dust claim either).
- **IP65 and IP64** on a few - dust-tight with jet or splash protection rather than immersion.
- **IP69** (and one IP68/IP69 dual listing) - high-pressure jet resistance, a rare claim.
- **No rating listed** on two phones. Absence of a rating is not a rating; treat undocumented as unknown, never as waterproof.

## Why foldables carry different numbers

A folding hinge cannot be sealed the way a solid frame can: it has to move, thousands of times, and dust that enters the hinge mechanism is a mechanical problem rather than an electrical one. That is why the foldables in our database show IP48 or IPX8 instead of the IP68 their slab siblings carry. For a foldable, the honest reading is "water resistance is comparable, dust resistance is not" - and dust is the more likely enemy of the hinge over years of ownership.

## How ratings degrade

A rating is a statement about the day it was tested. Seals age with heat cycles and time; drops deform frames; adhesive around the display can lift. None of this happens overnight, and none of it is visible from the outside. Practical habits that preserve it: avoid charging while the port is wet, dry the phone before it goes into a case, and skip the beach - fine sand and salt water are the two environments no rating addresses well.

## Practical rules

- Fresh water only, and only if you must - a pool, the sea, a hot shower and a sauna are all outside the test conditions.
- Rinse a salt-water splash with fresh water immediately if the phone is rated for it, then dry it.
- Never assume a marketing phrase like "water resistant" equals a specific IP rating; look for the digits.
- If the phone has no listed rating, plan around water as you would with any unprotected device.

## Comparing phones on water resistance

Our product pages record the published rating exactly as the manufacturer states it - IP68, IP48, IP54, or a blank where none is documented - and the Spec Comparison tool puts those rows side by side for any two models. The comparison that matters is rarely between IP67 and IP68; it is between a phone that claims immersion and one that only claims splash resistance, which is a different decision entirely.
